derivations.claim: Fix $D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ and define $q_D(x)=x^TDx$ on $S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x^Tx=1\}$. The sphere is nonempty, closed because $x\mapsto x^Tx$ is continuous, and bounded because each $|x_i|\le1$ there. The function $q_D$ is continuous because it is a finite sum of coordinate products. By [F1], $q_D$ has a maximum at some $e\in S^2$.

Let $X=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,d_2,d_3)$. The proper half-turns $Q_1=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1)$, $Q_2=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,-1)$, and $Q_3=\operatorname{diag}(-1,-1,1)$ each leave $X$ fixed. Equivariance gives $L(X)=Q_iL(X)Q_i^T$ for each $i$; because $L(X)$ is symmetric, these three equalities force every off-diagonal entry to vanish.

Let $y\in S^2$ satisfy $e^Ty=0$ and put $c(t)=(e+ty)/\sqrt{1+t^2}$. Then $c(t)^Tc(t)=1$ and differentiating at $0$ gives $c'(0)=y$. The differentiable function $t\mapsto q_D(c(t))$ has a maximum at $0$, so its derivative there is $0$: its right difference quotients are nonpositive and its left difference quotients are nonnegative. Differentiating gives $0=y^TDe+e^TDy=2y^TDe$, since $D^T=D$. By scaling, this holds for every $y\perp e$, so $De$ is a scalar multiple of $e$.

Let $E_{jj}$ be the diagonal matrix with a $1$ in position $(j,j)$ and $0$ elsewhere, and let the $j$th column of a matrix $M$ be the diagonal vector $(L(E_{jj})_{11},L(E_{jj})_{22},L(E_{jj})_{33})^T$. Linearity and step 1.2 give $\operatorname{diag}L(X)=M(d_1,d_2,d_3)^T$, where $\operatorname{diag}A=(A_{11},A_{22},A_{33})^T$. A permutation matrix $P$ permutes the coordinate basis; if $\det P=-1$, then $-P\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$ and $(-P)X(-P)^T=PXP^T$. Equivariance says $\operatorname{diag}L(PXP^T)=\operatorname{diag}(PL(X)P^T)$, hence $MPd=PMd$ for every vector $d$ and $MP=PM$. Equivalently $M_{ij}=M_{\pi(i)\pi(j)}$ for every permutation $\pi$, so its diagonal entries have a common value $c$ and its off-diagonal entries have a common value $d_0$. Thus $L(X)=(c-d_0)X+d_0(\operatorname{tr}X)I$.

If $z\perp e$, then $e^TDz=(De)^Tz=0$, so $e^\perp$ is invariant under $D$, and the restriction of $D$ to this two-dimensional plane is symmetric. Its unit circle is a nonempty closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^3$; repeating the argument of steps 1.1 and 2.1 on this invariant plane gives a unit eigenvector in $e^\perp$. The remaining one-dimensional orthogonal complement is invariant and consists of eigenvectors. Hence $D$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis. Only finitely many vectors are chosen in this construction; no arbitrary choice principle is used.

By step 3.1 write an arbitrary $D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ as $D=OXO^T$ with $O$ orthogonal and $X$ diagonal. If $\det O=-1$, change the sign of one eigenvector; this changes $\det O$ to $1$ and leaves $OXO^T$ unchanged. We may therefore take $O\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$. Equivariance and step 2.2 yield $L(D)=(c-d_0)D+d_0(\operatorname{tr}D)I$.

Set $2\mu=c-d_0$ and $\lambda=d_0$. Conversely, for any real $\lambda,\mu$, the map $D\mapsto2\mu D+\lambda(\operatorname{tr}D)I$ is linear and equivariant: $QIQ^T=I$, and $\operatorname{tr}(QDQ^T)=\sum_{j,k=1}^3D_{jk}\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ij}Q_{ik}=\sum_{j=1}^3D_{jj}=\operatorname{tr}D$ because the columns of $Q$ are orthonormal. If two coefficient pairs give the same map, evaluation at $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,0)$ makes their $2\mu$ coefficients equal, and evaluation at $I$ then makes their $\lambda$ coefficients equal. This proves existence, converse, and uniqueness.

derivations.claim: Put $f(v,s)=e_s(v,s)$ and $a_0=e_{ss}(v_0,s_0)>0$. Since $U$ is open and $e_{ss},e_{sv}$ are continuous, choose $\delta,\rho>0$ so the closed rectangle $R=[v_0-\delta,v_0+\delta]\times[s_0-\rho,s_0+\rho]$ is contained in $U$, $f_s=e_{ss}\ge a_0/2=:a>0$ on $R$, and $|f_v|=|e_{sv}|\le B$ on $R$ for some finite $B$. By [F2] on the two vertical segments, $f(v_0,s_0-\rho)\le T_0-a\rho<T_0<T_0+a\rho\le f(v_0,s_0+\rho)$. Continuity of the endpoint values in $v$ therefore gives smaller open intervals $V$ about $v_0$ and $J$ about $T_0$, with $J\subset(0,\infty)$, such that $f(v,s_0-\rho)<T<f(v,s_0+\rho)$ for all $(v,T)\in V\times J$.

For fixed $v\in V$, [F2] and $f_s\ge a$ imply that $s\mapsto f(v,s)$ is strictly increasing on $[s_0-\rho,s_0+\rho]$. By [F3], for every $T\in J$ there is $s(v,T)\in(s_0-\rho,s_0+\rho)$ with $f(v,s(v,T))=T$; strict increase gives uniqueness in that interval.

Take $(v,T),(v',T')\in V\times J$ and write $s=s(v,T)$, $s'=s(v',T')$. Applying [F2] in the $s$ variable and using $f_s\ge a$ gives $a|s'-s|\le|f(v,s')-f(v,s)|=|f(v,s')-T|$. Since $f(v',s')=T'$, [F2] in the $v$ variable and $|f_v|\le B$ give $|f(v,s')-T|\le B|v-v'|+|T-T'|$. Hence $s(v,T)$ is locally Lipschitz and, in particular, continuous.

At a fixed $(v,T)$, let $h,k$ be increments in $v,T$ and set $\Delta s=s(v+h,T+k)-s(v,T)$. The bound of step 3.1 gives $\Delta s=O(|h|+|k|)$. By the definition of the total derivative of the $C^1$ function $f$ at $(v,s(v,T))$, $k=f_vh+f_s\Delta s+o(|h|+|\Delta s|)$, so $\Delta s=-\frac{f_v}{f_s}h+\frac1{f_s}k+o(|h|+|k|)$. Thus $s_v=-e_{sv}/e_{ss}$ and $s_T=1/e_{ss}$. These derivatives are continuous because $e$ has continuous total derivatives through order two, $s$ is continuous, and $e_{ss}\ge a>0$; therefore the unique local branch is continuously differentiable.
By [F4] and the identity $e_s(v,s(v,T))=T$, differentiation of $a=e(v,s(v,T))-T s(v,T)$ gives $a_v=e_v+(e_s-T)s_v=e_v=-p$ and $a_T=e_s s_T-s-Ts_T=-s$.

Differentiating the first-derivative identities of step 5.1 and using step 4.1 yields $a_{TT}=-s_T=-1/e_{ss}$ and $a_{vv}=\partial_v(e_v(v,s(v,T)))=e_{vv}+e_{vs}s_v=e_{vv}-e_{vs}e_{sv}/e_{ss}$. These derivatives are continuous by the stated regularity, so $a$ is $C^2$. All derivatives are evaluated at the chart point $(v,s(v,T))$.

derivations.claim: Under the conditional Gibbs identity [F1] and the countable-choice premise [A2, F3], substituting the stress and flux expressions assumed in the Statement, with $g=\nabla T$, identifies $\mathcal Q$ with the entropy residual. The stress expression is a member of the linear isotropic family classified by [F2]; that classification imposes no sign condition on its coefficients. The trace of $D_0$ is $\theta-\frac{\theta}{3}\operatorname{tr}I=0$, and $D=D_0+\frac{\theta}{3}I$.

Since $D_0:I=\operatorname{tr}D_0=0$ and $I:I=3$, contraction gives $\tau:D=2\mu|D_0|^2+\left(\lambda+\frac{2\mu}{3}\right)\theta^2=2\mu|D_0|^2+\zeta\theta^2$. Also $-q\cdot g=g^TKg=g^T(\operatorname{sym}K)g$: the scalar $g^T(K-K^T)g$ equals its transpose $g^T(K^T-K)g$, so it is zero. Hence $\mathcal Q(D,g,T)=(2\mu|D_0|^2+\zeta\theta^2)/T+g^T(\operatorname{sym}K)g/T^2$.
If $\mu\ge0$, $\zeta\ge0$, and $\operatorname{sym}K$ is positive semidefinite, every term in step 2.1 is nonnegative for all $D,g,T>0$. This proves sufficiency.
For necessity, take $T=1$, $g=0$, and $D=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,0)$. Then $\theta=0$, $D_0=D$, and $|D_0|^2=2$, so step 2.1 gives $\mathcal Q=4\mu\ge0$ and hence $\mu\ge0$.
Take $T=1$, $g=0$, and $D=I/3$. Then $\theta=1$ and $D_0=0$, so $\mathcal Q=\zeta\ge0$.
Take $T=1$, $D=0$, and arbitrary $g\in\mathbb R^3$. Then $\mathcal Q=g^T(\operatorname{sym}K)g\ge0$ for every $g$, which is exactly positive semidefiniteness of $\operatorname{sym}K$.

If $\mu>0$ and $\zeta=0$, then $\lambda=-2\mu/3<0$, while step 3.1 still gives nonnegative residual whenever $\operatorname{sym}K$ is positive semidefinite. Thus nonnegativity of $\lambda$ is not necessary.
